newsitem.title: ITALY: FORECAST - Italy seen cutting key rate 75 bp end-Nov.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Italy seen cutting key rate 75 bp end-Nov.

text.p: The Bank of Italy could cut its key discount rate by 75 basis points at the end of November if annual CPI falls below three percent and passage of the 1997 budget is on track, a Reuter poll of 11 leading analysts showed.

The quarterly survey, conducted in the week of October 7, forecast that 10-year government bond (Btp) yields should hold around 8.30 percent, in line with current levels, then ease during the first half of next year.
The average forecast for the fourth quarter 1996 10-year Btp/Bund spread, currently around 230 basis points, shows a dip to 215 bps and below 200 bps by mid-1997.

Economists polled saw inflation data as the main trigger for Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio to cut the discount rate for the second time since he ended a 14-month freeze on July 24, when the rate was lowered to 8.25 percent from 9.0 percent.

The average forecast saw a cut of 75 basis points to 7.50 percent by the end of the year, with a further 25 basis point easing in the first quarter, and a fall to 7.0 percent by mid-year. It anticipated no further change for the rest of 1997.
"I see a reduction of 75 basis points at the end of November after the budget and when CPI is below three percent," said Martino Dolfini at Chase Manhattan Bank.

The budget debate is due to end in the (lower) Chamber of Deputies by November 17 and must be passed by both houses of parliament by the end of the year. The centre-left government controls the Senate (upper house) and hopes the budget can be passed there swiftly and without problems by early December.
"I think the first cut will come around November 20 because the cities' preliminary CPI data is released around that time," said Francesco Giordano at San Paolo Bank in London.
In his forecast, the most bullish, he expected a 75 basis points cut at that time then a 50 bps easing by the end of the year, following approval of the 1997 budget.
At the opposite end of the spectrum, Daniele Castelnuovo, chief economist at Banca Euromobiliare, saw Italy's efforts to join European monetary union restraining the pace of rate cuts.
"Italy won't enter the single currency at the start so the Bank of Italy will have to continue a strict monetary policy to keep inflation very low," Castelnuovo said.

"The Bank of Italy will be forcing Italian companies to try to become more competitive by keeping the exchange rate and interest rates as high as possible, so that when Italy goes in (to the single currency) the real economy will be as competitive as possible," he added.

Giordano said that unless the Bank of Italy acted to trim rates by the first quarter next year, its window of opportunity to do so might close because he forecast upward pressure on German rates and a hike by the Fed in the United States.
"I have a very strong feeling that even though the Bank of Italy can tighten when others are easing, the other way round would be impossible," he said.
